item.title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature — Tue Oct 20 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Tue Oct 20 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Tue Oct 20 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. item.title: Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge — Tue Oct 20 — Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University
item.description: For more than a decade, Indiana-born Samuel Levi Jones has created abstract assemblages with found printed and bound matter, deconstructing encyclopedias, law books, medical texts, and other didactic materials. Jones removes their fabric covers and pulps their pages, sewing these swatches together and applying paper pulp to create texturally rich, collaged works with raw edges, loose threads, and worn surfaces. His process of physically destroying archival materials and reconstructing them into artworks constitutes a materially engaged critique of institutional authority, reflecting on systems of knowledge that uphold power and privilege in the United States. For his exhibition at the Eskenazi Museum, Jones mined the museum’s collection for works that resonate with the themes he interrogates, including nationalism and patriotism, censorship, and the representation marginalized identities in historical narratives. item.description: Spanning more than 150 years, The Photographic Reflex celebrates a transformative gift to the Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University: more than one hundred works by eighty artists, generously donated by Lee Marks and John C. DePrez Jr. This exhibition features photographs dating from 1856 to 2017 and highlights the medium’s extraordinary range, both as a tool for documentation and as a vehicle for artistic exploration. From Alfred Stieglitz’s delicate studies of grass to Richard Misrach’s vast images of the cosmos, photographers have long found inspiration in the natural world. The built environment has also served as a compelling subject, and the exhibition includes Berenice Abbott’s striking views of 1920s New York City as well as Edward Burtynsky’s sweeping industrial landscapes. item.title: Safety Cabaret (Load-Out) — Tue Oct 20, 9:00 AM — Buskirk-Chumley Theater
item.description:
October 20, 9am – 5pm: Load-Out Load-Out will examine the production process in reverse. Participants will see how quickly a theatre changes when equipment begins coming down, scenery starts moving, cables are removed, rigging systems are operating, and areas that were safe during a performance become active work zones. Load-out also provides another opportunity for departments to better understand one another’s priorities. The sequence in which equipment comes down matters. Access needed by one department may affect the work of another. Schedule pressure and fatigue can make communication even more important. Participants will be able to see how planning, coordination, and mutual understanding can make load-out both safer and more efficient.
Participants may register for individual days or the full three-day event. Registration and additional event information: https://delong.ludus.com/show_page.php?show_id=200534364 https://delong.ludus.com/show_page.php?show_id=200534364

item.title: Community Forum: Vaccines in a Changing Political Climate — Tue Oct 20, 5:00 PM — Monroe County Public Library
item.description:
Presented by Concerned Scientists @ IU, Advocates for Science @ IU, Please join us at the Monroe County Public Library Auditorium on October 20 for “Vaccines in a Changing Political Climate.” The panel discussion and community forum will feature three vaccine policy experts, Dr. Katharine Head (Department of Communication, IU Indianapolis), Lisa Robertson, MPH (Executive Director, Indiana Immunization Coalition), and James Laughlin, MD (Riley Pediatric Primary Care (retired), Adjunct Clinical Professor, IU Medical School) — to discuss the state of science and politics and policy of vaccines in an era of politicization of medical care. The program will take place from 5:00 - 6:30 PM on Tuesday, October 20 at the Monroe County Public Library. For those who are unable to join us in person, the program will also be live-streamed from the ASIU YouTube channel: https://www.youtube.com/@AdvocatesforScienceatIU.

item.title: The Good Funeral — Death, Grief, and the Community of Care — Tue Oct 20, 7:30 PM — Presidents Hall in Franklin Hall
item.description:
Having spent more than half a century as a funeral director, Thomas Lynch has observed many changes in the funeral and the species that enacts it. This lecture will seek to address the widespread curiosity, amplified by the growing mortality among the baby boom generation, about the ever-changing cultural landscape of end-of-life activities, traditions and procedures, mortuary customs, and funeral practices. By promulgating a workable definition for the funeral and distinguishing it from other terms associated with a death in the community, The Good Funeral will proffer a mission statement, a list of essential elements, and a further discussion of the human response to death and loss. It will include a discussion of religious dynamics and forms of body disposition with particular attention on the theory and practice of cremation.
Source: Visit Bloomington

item.title: Yonder Mountain String Band — Wed Oct 21, 7:00 PM — Buskirk-Chumley Theater
item.description: Grammy-nominated Yonder Mountain String Band set the tone for a new way forward in acoustic music, carrying bluegrass into rooms and conversations it had never reached before. Nearly three decades later, that same spirit still guides them, alive and present on Good As True (2026), the band’s 12th studio album, arriving March 27th, 2026. The record captures Yonder in full stride. It’s unguarded and in motion, preserving the spark of musicians playing in real time and leaning into everything they have learned along the way. Good As True (2026) digs into communication, the conversations that carry us forward and the ones that fall apart. The things we say, the things we mean, and what gets lost in between. “Brand New Heartache,” the album’s lead single, lives in that fragile moment after a breakup when heartbreak and forward motion exist at the same time. item.title: Prime Minister w/Q&A | Additional Films and Guests — Wed Oct 21, 7:00 PM — IU CINEMA
item.description:
This gripping documentary chronicles Jacinda Ardern navigating unprecedented national tragedies, a volcanic eruption, and a global pandemic as New Zealand's youngest female leader. By balancing immense political pressure with first-time motherhood, she redefines global leadership through an empathetic yet resolute approach. Packed with raw audio diaries and candid footage, this film delivers a powerful, inspiring portrait of a woman who proved that vulnerability and unyielding strength can rewrite the rules of power. [101 min; documentary; English]A Q&A will follow the screening. Co-sponsored by the Center of Excellence for Women & Technology and the Office of the Vice Provost for Faculty and Academic Affairs.

item.title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature — Thu Oct 22 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment — Thu Oct 22 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment examines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU

item.title: The Declaration of Independence: The Signers — Thu Oct 22 — LILLY LIBRARY
item.description: IU Libraries Lilly Library invites you to The Declaration of Independence: The Signers, an exhibition of letters and documents bearing the autographs of the fifty-six men who signed the August 2, 1776 handwritten copy of the Declaration. Though the length and content of these letters and documents vary widely, from brief notes or orders to long and detailed personal letters, they all offer insight into the daily lives, activities, and concerns of the signers. One aspect of their lives that these documents don't reveal, however, is the ownership of slaves by a great many of the signers, which is discussed in the "Race, Slavery, and Native Americans" section of the exhibition in the Lilly Library's North Gallery, The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Moment. (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library/declaration-independence) Documents signed by fifty-four of the fifty-six signers are displayed in the Lilly Library's South Gallery. item.title: Samuel Levi Jones: An Archaeology of Knowledge — Thu Oct 22 — Eskenazi Museum of Art at Indiana University
item.description: For more than a decade, Indiana-born Samuel Levi Jones has created abstract assemblages with found printed and bound matter, deconstructing encyclopedias, law books, medical texts, and other didactic materials. Jones removes their fabric covers and pulps their pages, sewing these swatches together and applying paper pulp to create texturally rich, collaged works with raw edges, loose threads, and worn surfaces. His process of physically destroying archival materials and reconstructing them into artworks constitutes a materially engaged critique of institutional authority, reflecting on systems of knowledge that uphold power and privilege in the United States. For his exhibition at the Eskenazi Museum, Jones mined the museum’s collection for works that resonate with the themes he interrogates, including nationalism and patriotism, censorship, and the representation marginalized identities in historical narratives. item.title: THURSDAY MUSIC NIGHT: THE HOT CLUB OF BTOWN! — Thu Oct 22, 6:00 PM — Juniper Art Gallery
item.description:
Juniper is thrilled to host an evening of fabulous Jazz Manouche with the new quartet, The Hot Club of Btown! Featured musicians are Steve Mascari, Ingrid Matthews, Alan Bent, and Craig Coley.
A brief definition of this genre of music:
Jazz manouche is a musical idiom inspired by the Romani jazz guitarist Jean "Django" Reinhardt (1910–1953), in conjunction with the French jazz violinist Stéphane Grappelli (1908–1997), as expressed by their group the Quintette du Hot Club de France. The style has its origins in France and the Manouche clan of Romanis and has remained popular amongst this clan.
This is sure to be an evening filled with truly exceptional music that will uplift all in attendance! Do not miss this performance!

item.title: No Prisoners — a genre-bending work in words — Thu Oct 22, 7:30 PM — Presidents Hall in Franklin Hall
item.description:
Having produced and published poems, essays, short and long fiction, and drama, Thomas Lynch will discuss the various genres of literary expression and how his own work in words has taken shape over the past fifty years. This lecture will include brief samples of poetry, literary non-fiction, and his debut novel, all under the one title of “No Prisoners” – each an effort to tell his father’s story as a combat Marine, fighting in the South Pacific, during World War II. It will further investigate how the telling of our parents’ stories, in an effort to better understand how we come to be the ones we are, eventually becomes the telling of our own stories.
Source: Visit Bloomington

item.description:
The term Mehendi is the Indian word for Henna, and it is also the term used to describe the art of applying henna. Come and learn the basic designs and application techniques of Henna or Mehendi, which is used to create temporary tattoos. Please feel free to bring your friends to learn more about Desi culture and the significance of Mehendi in the Indian culture! If you come with a group of more than 7 members, please email acc@iu.edu in advance so we can prepare the henna materials. All Indiana University events, groups, activities, and educational, cultural, and historical observances welcome all IU students and other members of the Indiana University community.
